prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

The central median of urban arterial roads with a design speed higher than 60 km/h shall be densely planted with evergreen plants to avoid glare interference from oncoming traffic at night. 70 b. Within the range of 0.6 m to 1.5 m above the surface of the adjacent motor vehicle roadway, the plants configured shall have dense foliage throughout the year, and their spacing shall not be greater than 5 times the canopy spread. c. The width of the central median shall be 1.5 m or more, and a formal arrangement structure shall be adopted; simple repetition is preferable to create rhythm. At intersections and important nodes, plants shall mainly be low shrubs; planting trees is strictly prohibited to avoid tree trunks causing glare and traffic accidents. Figure 3.3-1 Schematic diagram of central median B. Side median a. Where the width of the side green belt between carriageways is greater than or equal to 1.5 m, trees shall be the main planting type, and trees, shrubs, and groundcover plants should be combined. The canopies of trees on both sides should not overlap above the motor vehicle lanes. b. Where the width of the side green belt between carriageways is less than 1.5 m, shrubs shall be the main planting type, and shrubs and groundcover plants should be combined. 71 Figure 3.3-2 Schematic diagram of central median C. It is encouraged to set up Suzhou-specific rockery stones and pruned topiary forms, creating a regional garden-style landscape with varied stone forms, distinct layers of vegetation, and brightly colored flowers. c. Building Appearance 1) Typical problems: The overall appearance of buildings in streets and lanes is uncoordinated; shop signs are dilapidated and lack distinctiveness; colors are inconsistent; nighttime lighting design is unreasonable; walls are damaged and dirty; outdoor air-conditioning units and facade pipelines are cluttered, etc. 2) Renewal guidelines 【Appearance Improvement】 Clean and repair building facades along the street to ensure they are neat and clean. The color and style of street building facades should coordinate with the surrounding environment, and local characteristic materials should be selected where appropriate to highlight regional features. Encourage quality improvement of ground-floor facades along the street, shop signs and shop boards, and facades around areas where people mainly gather and move, in combination with pedestrian perspectives and walking scale. Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Vehicle Traffic System 2 Vehicle Traffic System 2.1 Vehicle Traffic Space Scale The longitudinal and transverse road space occupied by vehicular traffic is referred to as vehicle traffic space. Generally speaking, vehicle traffic space includes carriageways, bus-only lanes, medians, and roadside parking lanes. Figure 2.1-1 Components of Vehicle Traffic Space 2.1.1 Motor Vehicle Lane The width of a motor vehicle lane shall include the carriageway width and the curb lane widths on both sides. Where a single carriageway road or a three-carriageway road uses a central separator or double yellow lines to separate opposing traffic, the pavement width of the motor vehicle lane shall also include the width of the separator or double yellow lines. 1. Running Lane The width of a running lane is related to the road design speed. The recommended width for urban road running lanes is 3.25 m–3.5 m. 2. Two-Way Single Lane Where a lower-grade branch road is designed as a single lane permitting two-way travel, the width shall be 4.5 m. The subgrade width for sections with passing bays shall not be less than 6.5 m. 3. Bus-Only Lane The recommended width of a bus-only lane is 3.5 m. At bus stops, the lane width shall be 3 m. 27 Figure 2.1-2 Typical Lane Width Settings 2.1.2 Tidal Lane In response to the “tidal phenomenon” of traffic, lanes may be provided on road sections whose direction of travel can be changed according to traffic flow demand. In addition, the control center may monitor intersection conditions through instruments and, when appropriate, use remote control means to control signboards; where intersection signal controllers are connected in a computer network, they may also be identified through an automatic recognition system and automatically regulated. A “time-limited pedestrian street” form may also be adopted, whereby motor vehicle access is prohibited during specified periods on part of the road, and a high-quality block combining commerce and culture is created in conjunction with the characteristics of the road section. 2.1.4 Median The median shall be enclosed with curb stones. Where anti-collision requirements need to be considered, anti-collision guardrails of the corresponding grade shall be used. When rainwater detention facilities need to be installed in the road median, the curb stone arrangement shall meet drainage requirements. 2.1.5 Bus-Only Lane 1. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 3 lanes or more (including 3 lanes), or the total one-way motor vehicle roadway width is not less than 11 m; where one-way passenger bus volume on the road section exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, or bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour; and where the average section flow per lane exceeds 500 vehicles/peak hour. 2. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 4 lanes or more (including 4 lanes), and the one-way bus flow on the section exceeds 90 vehicles/peak hour. 3. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 2 lanes, the one-way passenger bus volume exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, and bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour. 29 4. Bus-only lanes may be paved with colored asphalt. After paving, the lane color is conspicuous and forms a sharp contrast with the adjacent ordinary motor vehicle lane, preventing ordinary motor vehicles from mistakenly entering the lane.
